opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think those are two really nice examples of what people now call inference-time scaling, where instead of making the model bigger or training it longer, you spend more compute when you actually generate the answer.

Self-consistency is probably the simplest one conceptually. You sample multiple answers from the model, usually with some temperature so you get diversity, and then you pick the answer that comes up most often, basically majority voting. What I like about it is that it's really easy to implement. You don't need to change the model at all, and for tasks with a clear final answer, like math problems or multiple choice, it works surprisingly well. The downside is cost, since generating ten or twenty answers means paying for ten or twenty times the tokens. It also only really works when you can compare answers. For open-ended writing there's no clean way to vote.

Self-refinement is a bit different. Instead of sampling in parallel, it's sequential. The model generates an answer, then critiques it, then revises it based on that critique, and you can repeat that a few times. It's appealing because it resembles how we work ourselves: you write a draft, look at it again, and fix things. In practice it's more mixed, though. If the model can't recognize its own mistakes, it can just confidently rewrite a correct answer into a wrong one, or keep making cosmetic changes. It tends to work much better with some external signal, like running code against unit tests or using a separate verifier, instead of relying purely on the model judging itself.

So I see them as complementary. Self-consistency is kind of a breadth approach and self-refinement is a depth approach. A lot of the more recent reasoning models internalize some of this. They're trained to produce long chains of thought where they backtrack and check their work, so part of that refinement happens inside one generation. Still, I think these explicit techniques are really useful, especially if you're working with a smaller open-weight model and want to squeeze out more performance without retraining. You just have to be mindful of the compute budget, because past a certain point the returns diminish pretty quickly.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's useful to put these two into a broader framework first. When people talk about scaling inference, there are really two big families of approaches. One is where you make the model generate more and then pick from what it generated, and the other is where you give the model a chance to go back and fix its own output. Self-consistency falls into the first bucket, self-refinement into the second.

Self-consistency is conceptually very simple, and I think that's actually its strength. You sample multiple chain-of-thought reasoning paths for the same question, usually with a non-zero temperature so you get some diversity, and then you take a majority vote over the final answers. The intuition is that there are many ways to reason correctly toward the right answer, but wrong reasoning paths tend to scatter and disagree with each other. So the correct answer should show up more often if you sample enough. And empirically that holds up quite well on things like math and multiple-choice reasoning benchmarks. The limitation is pretty obvious, though. You need a final answer you can actually vote over. If the task is writing an essay or generating code where there's no single canonical output, majority voting doesn't really apply, and you'd have to fall back to something like a verifier or reward model to score the candidates instead. The other thing is cost. If you sample forty paths, you're paying forty times the compute, and the gains tend to saturate after a certain point.

Self-refinement is a bit more interesting to me, and also a bit more controversial. The idea is you let the model produce an answer, then prompt it to critique that answer and produce a revised version, potentially iterating a few times. Papers like Self-Refine showed nice improvements on certain tasks. But then there was follow-up work, including the "Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet" paper, that pointed out something important. If you don't give the model any external signal, like a unit test result or ground truth, then intrinsic self-correction on reasoning tasks often doesn't help and can even make things worse. The model may change a correct answer to an incorrect one simply because you asked it to reconsider. So the honest assessment, I think, is that self-refinement works well when there's some external feedback loop, code execution being the classic example, and it's much shakier when the model is purely judging itself.

So if I had to summarize, self-consistency is reliable but expensive and narrow in applicability, and self-refinement is broader in applicability but fragile without external verification. And I'd say both of these are somewhat being absorbed into the newer reasoning models, where the exploration and the self-checking happen inside the model's own chain of thought via reinforcement learning training rather than being orchestrated from the outside. But as inference-time techniques you can apply to any off-the-shelf model, they're still very much worth understanding.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re two useful ways to spend more compute at inference time, but they make different assumptions. With self-consistency, you ask the model to solve the same problem multiple times, sample different reasoning paths, and then take the most common answer. The intuition is that there can be many ways to arrive at the right answer, while mistakes might lead you in different directions. It works particularly well when you have a clear final answer that you can compare across samples, like a math problem.

The limitation is that those errors aren’t necessarily independent. If the model has a systematic misconception, you can get the same wrong answer repeatedly. So agreement is a useful signal, but it isn’t a guarantee of correctness. And, of course, you’re paying for multiple generations.

Self-refinement is more sequential: you generate an answer, ask the model to critique it, and then revise it. That’s appealing, but the key question is: can the model recognize a mistake it couldn’t avoid making in the first place? Sometimes it can, especially if you give it concrete criteria to check. But simply saying, ‘Think again,’ can also cause it to change a correct answer into an incorrect one.

I’m more optimistic about refinement when there’s external feedback—for example, running generated code and using test failures to guide the next attempt. Then you have a signal beyond the model’s own judgment. So I’d assess both approaches by how much additional accuracy they buy for the extra compute and latency, and by how reliably you can select or verify the result.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re two useful ways of spending more compute at inference time, but they make different bets. With self-consistency, you generate several reasoning paths and then look for agreement in the final answer. The intuition is that there may be many ways to arrive at the correct answer, while mistakes are more scattered. That works particularly well when you can compare answers reliably, like in a math problem.

Self-refinement is more sequential. You generate an answer, ask the model to critique it, and then revise it. The challenge is that generating an answer and recognizing whether it’s correct aren’t necessarily the same capability. If the model has a misconception, asking it to think again may just reinforce that misconception—or cause it to change a correct answer into an incorrect one.

So I’m more optimistic about refinement when there’s useful feedback: a test result, a tool, or some other way to check the answer. In both cases, the question is whether the additional compute buys you better accuracy. More samples or more revision steps don’t automatically mean better reasoning.
